name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

questions.questionText: The photoelectric effect demonstrates:
questions.solution: Photoelectric effect shows light behaves as particles (photons).

questions.questionText: Einstein's photoelectric equation is:
questions.solution: KE_max = hv - phi where phi is work function.

questions.questionText: The threshold frequency is the minimum frequency:
questions.optionB: Below which no photoelectrons are emitted
questions.solution: Below threshold frequency photon energy < work function, no emission.

questions.questionText: Stopping potential depends on:
questions.solution: Stopping potential depends on max KE which depends on frequency, not intensity.

questions.questionText: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum p is:
questions.solution: de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p.

questions.questionText: Work function of a metal is:
questions.optionB: Minimum energy needed to remove an electron
questions.solution: Work function phi is the minimum energy to extract an electron from the metal surface.

questions.questionText: Increasing intensity of light above threshold frequency:
questions.solution: Higher intensity means more photons, so more electrons emitted.

questions.questionText: The energy of a photon of frequency v is:
questions.solution: E = hv (Planck's relation).

questions.questionText: de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts is:
questions.solution: KE = eV, p = sqrt(2meV), lambda = h/p = h/sqrt(2meV).

questions.questionText: Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed:
questions.solution: Davisson-Germer showed electron diffraction confirming wave nature.

questions.questionText: Photoelectric effect is instantaneous because:
questions.optionB: Energy transfer is in discrete quanta (photons)
questions.solution: One photon transfers all its energy to one electron instantly.

questions.questionText: The momentum of a photon of wavelength lambda is:
questions.solution: p = h/lambda for a photon.

questions.questionText: If the wavelength of incident light is halved, maximum KE of photoelectrons:
questions.solution: KE = hc/lambda - phi. Halving lambda doubles hc/lambda but phi is constant so KE more than doubles.

questions.questionText: Saturation current in photoelectric effect depends on:
questions.solution: Saturation current depends on number of photoelectrons which depends on intensity.

questions.questionText: The value of Planck's constant is approximately:
de Broglie hypothesis applies to:
questions.solution: de Broglie wavelength applies to all moving matter particles.

questions.questionText: Photoelectric current is proportional to:
questions.solution: More photons (intensity) means more electrons emitted.

questions.questionText: A photon has zero:
questions.solution: Photons are massless particles (zero rest mass) travelling at c.

questions.questionText: If frequency is doubled the stopping potential:
questions.solution: eV0 = hv - phi. Doubling v: eV0' = 2hv - phi > 2(hv - phi) = 2eV0.

questions.questionText: Electron microscope uses:
questions.solution: Electron microscope exploits short de Broglie wavelength of electrons for high resolution.

questions.questionText: The graph of stopping potential vs frequency is:
questions.solution: V0 = (h/e)v - phi/e: linear with positive slope h/e.

questions.questionText: The particle nature of radiation is confirmed by:
questions.solution: Photoelectric and Compton effects demonstrate particle (photon) nature.

questions.questionText: de Broglie wavelength is significant for:
questions.solution: lambda = h/mv. For macroscopic objects lambda is negligibly small. For electrons it is measurable.

questions.questionText: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states:
questions.optionA: Position and momentum can both be precisely known
questions.optionB: Product of uncertainties in position and momentum >= h/(4*pi)
questions.solution: Delta_x * Delta_p >= h/(4*pi).

questions.questionText: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. Threshold wavelength is:
questions.solution: lambda_0 = hc/phi = 1240 eV*nm / 2 eV = 620 nm.
